body.observations: E0 (default run r001) shows: udp_goodput_bps=300003200, udp_loss_frac=0.0, tcp_goodput_bps=668633114, drops_band1=92, tcp_retrans=92, link_util=1.0. With weightUdp=0.5, TCP goodput is far above a nominal 50% share, which suggests the scheduler is work-conserving and TCP can use UDP's unused configured capacity. The UDP application demands about 300 Mbps payload, so the UDP demand share is likely near 0.30-0.33 of the link depending on packet overhead. The key unknowns are: (1) how TCP goodput changes as weightUdp is lowered while UDP still has no loss, (2) where UDP loss begins as weightUdp falls below UDP demand, and (3) whether queue size or TCP variant changes the optimum.

body.observations: E0 and E1 show that with default settings the link is saturated (link_util=1.0) and UDP is delivered without loss at weightUdp=0.35, 0.40, 0.50. UDP loss appears when weightUdp is reduced: 0.30 gives udp_loss_frac=0.020944, 0.25 gives 0.184115, 0.20 gives 0.34729. TCP goodput increases as UDP loss increases: 674.82 Mbps at w030, 723.02 Mbps at w025, 771.23 Mbps at w020, while UDP goodput falls correspondingly. The sums udp_goodput_bps+tcp_goodput_bps are nearly constant around 968.6 Mbps across these runs. C1 held: tcp_goodput at w040 equals w050, supporting work-conserving scheduler behavior when UDP demand is below its configured share. C2 held: UDP loss crosses the 1% threshold between weightUdp=0.25 and 0.35. The r001 series shows TCP queue near its 100-packet limit with about 9 drops/s and UDP queue mostly empty, consistent with TCP being backlogged and UDP demand being served without loss at default weight.

When UDP is allowed to drop, TCP does not fully absorb the unused UDP share or overhead changes materially, so total delivered payload at these weights differs from the saturated reference by more than 2%.

body.observations: The default run and weight sweep show the scheduler is work-conserving: when weightUdp is at or above the UDP demand share, UDP loss is 0 and TCP goodput is about 668.63 Mbps. Below that, UDP loss rises and TCP goodput rises slightly because less UDP payload is delivered while the link remains saturated. The best feasible run so far is weightUdp=0.304, queuePkts=100, TcpCubic: tcp_goodput_bps=670962656 and udp_loss_frac=0.007888. weightUdp=0.306 is also feasible but gives lower TCP (669035078). queuePkts=1000 reduces UDP loss slightly at the same weight but lowers TCP goodput materially (663215718 at weightUdp=0.304), so larger queues are not automatically better for the objective. TcpBbr badly underfills the link (411354790 at weightUdp=0.35), while TcpNewReno matches TcpCubic at weightUdp=0.35. The 1% UDP-loss boundary for seed 1 and queuePkts=100 is between 0.302 and 0.304, and likely near 0.3033.

body.explanation: The scheduler is work-conserving: when UDP demand is below its configured share, TCP can use the unused UDP share, so TCP goodput is not simply capped by 1 - weightUdp (E1, C1, V1). UDP is offered at about 300 Mbps payload. With queuePkts=100 and TcpCubic, UDP loss becomes unacceptable below the measured boundary: weightUdp=0.3030 gives udp_loss_frac=0.011151, while weightUdp=0.3036 gives udp_loss_frac=0.009736, just below the 1% limit (E3, C7, V7). Because the link is saturated and total delivered payload is nearly constant (E2, C6, V6), TCP goodput is maximized by choosing the smallest configured UDP share that still satisfies the UDP-loss constraint. weightUdp=0.3036 is the lowest tested feasible weight and gives tcp_goodput_bps=671509421 at seed 1; it remains feasible for seeds 1-8, with udp_loss_frac between 0.009733 and 0.009736 and TCP goodput around 671.5 Mbps (E4, E5, C15). queuePkts=100 is the best tested queue size: queuePkts=4, 20, 50, and 200 do not improve TCP goodput materially, while queuePkts=1000 reduces TCP goodput and queuePkts=4 causes many TCP drops (E2, C3, V3, E3, C8, V8). TcpCubic is recommended because it fills the link; TcpBbr and TcpVegas materially underutilize it, and TcpLinuxReno, TcpNewReno, and TcpBic are not materially better than TcpCubic in the tested region (E2, C4, V4, E3, C9, V9). Seed and duration are not meaningful performance levers in the tested range; seed=1 and duration=10 are recommended for reproducibility, and any seed among 1-8 should give essentially the same result.
body.holds_when: The fixed system remains a single 1 Gbps link with 50 us one-way delay, 1500-byte MTU, a constant 300 Mbps UDP application sending 1400-byte packets, a greedy TCP sender, a work-conserving scheduler with separate UDP and TCP queues, and a measured steady-state window. The recommendation is supported for TcpCubic, queuePkts around 100, and seeds 1-8 tested here.
body.breaks_when: It would change if the UDP offered load changes, if the scheduler is not work-conserving, if the UDP-loss constraint is stricter than 1%, if queuePkts is made very large or very small, if a different TCP variant is required, if seeds beyond those tested shift the UDP-loss boundary, or if duration effects alter the measured steady-state average. A weight slightly below 0.3036 might be feasible if the exact boundary lies between 0.3030 and 0.3036, but it was not tested.

claims.text: The scheduler is work-conserving: TCP can use UDP capacity that UDP does not demand.
UDP loss appears when the configured UDP share is below the UDP demand share; with queuePkts=100 and TcpCubic the 1% UDP-loss boundary is between weightUdp=0.3030 and 0.3036.
At weightUdp=0.3036, queuePkts=100, TcpCubic, seed=1, udp_loss_frac=0.009736 <= 0.01 and tcp_goodput_bps=671509421.
In the saturated region, total delivered UDP plus TCP payload is nearly constant, so reducing the configured UDP share while keeping UDP loss <= 1% increases TCP goodput.

queuePkts=100 is preferable to very small or very large queues: larger queues do not materially reduce UDP loss and reduce TCP goodput, while very small queues cause TCP drops without improving TCP goodput.
TcpCubic is among the best TCP variants for this goal; TcpBbr and TcpVegas underutilize the link, and TcpLinuxReno, TcpNewReno, and TcpBic are not materially better than TcpCubic.
The recommended weightUdp=0.3036 is robust across seeds 1-8: udp_loss_frac remains <= 0.01 and TCP goodput remains about 671.5 Mbps.
weightUdp=0.304 is a robust fallback with udp_loss_frac=0.007888 across seeds 1-5 and tcp_goodput_bps about 670.96 Mbps.

open_questions: The exact 1% UDP-loss boundary between weightUdp=0.3030 and 0.3036 was not located; a value such as 0.3035 might be feasible.
The effect of duration values other than the default 10 seconds was not tested.
Seeds beyond 1-8 were not tested, although seed variation was very small in the tested range.
Whether TcpBic or another variant could give a tiny TCP gain at exactly weightUdp=0.3036 was not tested.
Whether queuePkts=200 or another moderate queue size could reduce TCP drops at weightUdp=0.3036 without changing goodput was not directly tested.
